title: Tell me about technical debt you inherited and how you handled it.
description: Learn how to answer the inherited technical debt interview question. Covers how to assess debt, prioritize paydown, communicate with stakeholders, and show strategic patience.

data.text: Every engineer inherits technical debt — it is the accumulated consequence of previous trade-offs, shortcuts, and changing requirements. Interviewers ask about inherited debt because they want to know if you can assess it calmly, prioritize it strategically, and pay it down without blocking all forward progress. A good answer shows that you treat debt as a business and technical problem, not just a personal annoyance.
What Inherited Technical Debt Looks Like

Inherited debt is not always obvious at first. It might be a module with no tests that everyone is afraid to touch, a database schema that no one fully understands, or an API that returns different data shapes depending on which client calls it. The first step is always assessment: you need to understand what the debt is, why it exists, and what it is actually costing the team before you can fix it.

items: No tests: Changes carry high risk because regressions are undetected
Unclear ownership: No one knows who should fix a problem when it arises
Spaghetti logic: Business rules are scattered, duplicated, or undocumented
Outdated dependencies: Libraries with security vulnerabilities or no maintainer support

data.text: Do not start by rewriting everything. The first step is to understand the cost of the debt by looking at incident frequency, change lead time, and how often the team avoids touching the affected code. Once you understand the cost, you can prioritize what to pay down first and build a case for allocating time to it alongside feature work.

items: Map the debt: Identify what the debt is, where it lives, and who is affected by it
Measure the cost: Track incidents, change failures, or time wasted working around it
Prioritize: Focus on the debt that is actively slowing the team or creating the most risk
Make the case: Explain to stakeholders what the debt costs and what paying it down will unlock
Pay down incrementally: Fix pieces of the debt alongside feature work, not in a big rewrite

data.text: Example: Refactoring an Unmaintainable Order Processing Module

A realistic debt scenario is inheriting a core business module that was written by a team that no longer exists, has no tests, and contains business logic that is duplicated across three services. Every change to order processing carries a high risk of breaking something in an unexpected place.

data.title: Sample Answer Outline
data.content:
I joined a team that maintained an order processing module written by engineers who had left the company. There were no unit tests, no documentation, and the same discount calculation logic was duplicated across three services. Every time we needed to change how discounts worked, we had to update all three places and manually verify the behavior.

I started by mapping the module: I read through the code, talked to the support team about common bugs, and tracked how many production incidents traced back to discount calculation errors. Over three months, I documented the bugs and their root causes. Six incidents, all caused by the duplicated logic.

I presented the data to my manager and the product team. I estimated that paying down the debt by centralizing the discount logic and adding tests would take about three weeks of focused work and would eliminate the class of bugs we had been seeing. The product team agreed to allocate one engineer for two sprints.

Instead of rewriting everything at once, I extracted the discount logic into a shared library, one service at a time, while continuing to ship features. Each extraction included tests and was validated in production with feature flags. Within two months, all three services were using the shared library, and we had not shipped a discount-related bug since.

The team eventually added the shared library to our onboarding checklist, so new engineers would not accidentally duplicate the logic again. The debt was not eliminated entirely — the module still had areas that needed tests — but the highest-risk part was resolved, and the team had a process for preventing it from recurring.

data.text: Interviewers want to see if you treat debt as a strategic problem rather than an emotional reaction. Do you assess the cost before proposing a fix? Do you communicate with stakeholders in terms they understand? And do you show patience — paying down debt incrementally rather than demanding a big rewrite that blocks all feature work?

terms.definition: Improving code structure in small steps alongside feature work instead of rewriting everything at once
The ongoing cost of technical debt — extra time spent working around poor design or fixing related bugs
A toggle that lets you ship code to production without exposing it to all users, enabling safe gradual rollout

data.title: Common Pitfall
data.text: Do not frame inherited debt as a personal insult or the result of incompetence. Interviewers are wary of engineers who blame previous teams. A mature answer acknowledges that the debt was likely the result of time pressure or changing requirements, not poor engineering.
When to Stop Paying Down Debt

You will never eliminate all technical debt, and that is okay. The goal is to reduce the debt that is actively costing the team more than it would cost to fix. If the debt is not causing incidents, not slowing feature delivery, and is well-understood, it may be better to leave it alone and invest your time elsewhere. Good engineering judgment means knowing when to act and when to accept the trade-off.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Start with assessment, not rewriting — understand the cost before proposing a fix
Use data to make your case to stakeholders: incidents, lead time, and bug frequency
Pay down debt incrementally alongside feature work
Never blame the previous team — focus on the systemic reason the debt accumulated
Not all debt needs to be paid down; prioritize the debt that is actively costing the team
